articles.title: Biden-appointed judge hands Letitia James setback in latest Trump legal clash
articles.summary: New York Attorney General Letitia James and 18 states lost their legal challenge after a federal judge dismissed the DOGE Treasury lawsuit as moot.
articles.body: New York Attorney General Letitia James’ legal battle against President Donald Trump over DOGE-linked access to sensitive Treasury systems ended Wednesday with a federal judge dismissing the lawsuit she spearheaded with 18 other states. The case stems from Trump’s January 2025 executive order establishing DOGE, which directed executive agencies to create DOGE teams and set July 4, 2026, as the termination date for the U.S. DOGE Service Temporary Organization. James led a coalition – which included New York and 18 other states – that sued the following month after Treasury gave DOGE-affiliated employees access to Bureau of the Fiscal Service systems, which process federal payments and contain sensitive financial information. JUDGE SAYS ISSUES IN TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ANTI-WEAPONIZATION CASE 'ALIVE AND KICKING' DESPITE DOJ PUSH Biden-appointed U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas ruled that the "plaintiffs’ claims related to access by DOGE-affiliated employees to sensitive Treasury information are dismissed as moot," according to Wednesday’s order. Vargas said the Treasury DOGE team had been disbanded, and no DOGE employees remained at Treasury, leaving no access practice for the court to enjoin. She separately dismissed the states’ claims over an automated payment-review system, finding they had not alleged that the process froze or canceled any specific federal payment due to them. The states argued the Trump administration unlawfully opened sensitive Treasury systems to DOGE, putting state financial information and federal payments at risk and exceeding the administration’s legal authority. EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE THE SECRETIVE MINE DOGE HELPED DRAG OUT OF A DECADES-OLD BUREAUCRATIC BLACK HOLE In February 2025, Vargas granted the states a preliminary injunction barring Treasury’s DOGE team from the covered payment systems, then modified the order over the following months to permit access for personnel who complied with specified vetting, training, hiring, reporting and mitigation procedures. The Executive Order established DOGE and called for each department to assemble its own DOGE team to find fraud, waste and abuse before their termination date of July 4. TRUMP'S LAWYERS PUT DEM AG ON NOTICE FOR TARGETING HIS FAMILY IN NY FRAUD FIGHT: 'CANNOT STAND' James has been a longtime critic and legal adversary of Trump, launching a civil fraud lawsuit against him and the Trump Organization in 2022 after campaigning on investigating his business practices. The case initially resulted in more than $450 million in penalties, though an appeals court later upheld Trump’s liability while voiding the financial penalty. articles.title: US appeals court reinstates Ohio law requiring voters to prove citizenship
articles.summary: By Luc Cohen Sept 24 (Reuters) - A US appeals court has for now reinstated an Ohio law requiring residents to present documentary proof of citizenship when r...
articles.body:
Sept 24 (Reuters) - A US appeals court has for now reinstated an Ohio law requiring residents to present ‌documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote at the ‌state's motor vehicle offices, in a boost for allies of President Donald Trump who want ​tighter voter registration rules.

• The 2-1 decision late on Wednesday by the Cincinnati-based 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals to pause a lower court ruling blocking the law was a win for Ohio's Republican government ahead ‌of the November 3 ⁠midterm elections.

• A competitive race for a Senate seat in Ohio is considered important for Democrats' hopes of ⁠regaining control of the Senate.

• Lawyers for the advocacy groups who challenged the law, Red Wine & Blue and the Ohio Alliance for Retired Americans, did ​not ​immediately respond to requests for comment.

• ​Trump and Republicans in state ‌governments across the country are pushing more restrictions on voter registration, based in part on unsubstantiated claims of widespread illegal voting by non-US citizens.

• Democrats and voting rights advocates counter that voting by non-US citizens is rare, and greater restrictions can make it harder for US citizens to vote.

• ‌In the Ohio case, Cleveland-based US District ​Judge Solomon Oliver Jr. in August granted ​a preliminary injunction blocking the ​state's 2025 law. He said that having voters ‌attest in writing that they are ​US citizens was ​sufficient to let Ohio election officials assess their eligibility to vote.

• In temporarily pausing Oliver's order, a three-judge 6th Circuit panel said ​advocacy groups that ‌challenged the law likely lacked standing, and that the order ​came too close to the election.

(Reporting by Luc Cohen in ​New York; Editing by Bill Berkrot)

articles.title: White House restores access to media outlets banned by Trump after judge's order
articles.summary: CNN, Politico and MS NOW were allowed back into the White House after some of their staff were earlier turned away.
articles.body:
CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters have been allowed back into the White House after they sought an emergency court hearing to restore their revoked press access.

They accused the White House in a court filing of having "repeatedly violated" a judge's order lifting President Donald Trump's ban on the three media outlets.

But the White House said in a filing that it began reinstating access shortly after 09:00 EDT (13:00 GMT) on Thursday.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico reported they were granted entry hours after some of their staff were turned away. Trump initially said he barred the outlets because of "fake news". The White House later cited national security.

In the early hours, Judge Timothy Kelly had ruled the ban on the outlets should be temporarily lifted because it "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".

The White House in its filing said that the press passes had been restored by 09:07 local time and that confiscated badges were available starting at 09:45.

The standoff limited some TV coverage as Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House ahead of a state dinner.

CNN said some of their journalists were denied entry, including senior White House reporter Betsy Klein. But a producer was allowed to enter, the outlet reported.

Politico said one of its reporters was denied access to the White House and had his press credentials confiscated.

MS NOW reported that its White House reporter Laura Barrón-López and a producer were barred and had their passes taken, but another MS NOW producer was allowed in.

Trump first announced last Friday he was barring CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.

By Saturday morning, each outlet reported that they were denied entry to the White House grounds and that their press badges were confiscated.

All three outlets spoke out against the ban, accusing the Trump administration of violating their constitutional rights.

In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports".

TV networks including Fox News, NBC, CBS and ABC had suspended their televised coverage of the White House in solidarity.

And more than 50 media organisations across the ideological spectrum filed an amicus brief in support of the lawsuit, including Fox News, the New York Times, the Washington Post and the Wall Street Journal.

There have been previous instances of administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.

The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a specific press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.

But after objections from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was allowed in.

articles.title: FAA: No political interference in Trump arch review
articles.summary: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) head Bryan Bedford said there was no political interference in the air safety review for President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch, which concluded that a visible eternal flame should be installed at the top of the structure. “We put the process through the same obstruction evaluation that our career [employees] do for…
articles.body:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) head Bryan Bedford said there was no political interference in the air safety review for President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch , which concluded that a visible eternal flame should be installed at the top of the structure.

“We put the process through the same obstruction evaluation that our career [employees] do for any project,” Bedford told reporters during a Wednesday event in Washington, Reuters reported .

The administrator added the FAA did not give the Trump-led project any special consideration during its review.

An FAA spokesperson told The Hill on Saturday the arch will be topped with a “non-standard eternal flame … and floodlight projectors pointed towards the Arch to make it noticeable for pilots.”

The agency also notified the National Park Service about the study and its lighting recommendations, which said the flame should “provide an average illumination of at least 15 foot-candles (161.46 lux) over the top one-third of the structure.”

The FAA released its hazard study on the project and confirmed the 250-foot arch “would not pose a hazard to aircraft” after examining air traffic patterns around Reagan Washington National Airport.

Structures standing more than 200 feet tall in Washington require lighting, although an “aeronautical study may reveal that the absence of marking and/or lighting will not impair aviation safety,” per FAA guidelines.

The Washington Monument, the tallest structure in the capital, features red obstruction lights close to the top of the 555-foot obelisk.

The arch would be located on the Arlington Memorial Bridge, which connects Washington to Arlington, Va. The bridge’s symbolism is tied to the country’s reunification after the Civil War, bridging the state that was home to the Confederate capital to the capital of the Union.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) on Tuesday challenged the president’s announcement that the arch would include a “ top grade military complex ” equipped with drones, snipers and “large quantities of sniper ammunition storage.” The lawmaker’s district includes Arlington and its National Cemetery.

“The overwhelming local opposition to Trump’s illegal and disrespectful vanity arch will not be defeated by this chicanery,” Beyer said in a statement . “The Narcissist in Chief is not fooling anyone.”

The triumphal arch would be the tallest in the world if completed, towering over the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and measuring 30 feet taller than the world’s tallest arch, the Monumento a la Revolución in Mexico City.

articles.title: Soros-linked prosecutor faces primary challenge as fellow Democrat targets his record
articles.summary: Fairfax County Commonwealth's Attorney Stephen Descano faces a Democratic primary challenge from a former federal prosecutor citing botched cases.
articles.body: Fairfax County Commonwealth’s Attorney Stephen Descano is facing a forceful rebuke from a former federal prosecutor who extensively criticized his record after announcing her bid to unseat him. Descano, a Democrat, has faced criticism over what opponents describe as lenient prosecutorial decisions, particularly in serious cases involving illegal immigrant suspects. Former federal prosecutor Brittany Dunn-Pirio said that if there weren’t systemic problems in his office, she would want to work there. "If this office were doing its job, I wouldn’t be running against it. I’d be applying to work for it. But it isn’t," Dunn-Pirio said on her new campaign website after Washington, D.C.-area media reported her bid late Wednesday. VIRGINIA DEMS SPLIT ON DOJ PROBE OF SOROS-BACKED DA ACCUSED OF GIVING 'SWEETHEART DEALS' TO ILLEGAL ALIENS "I’m a Democrat. This race isn’t about whether reform was right. It’s about whether the office can tell the difference between a first-time nonviolent offender who deserves a second chance and a violent or sexual offender who doesn’t," Dunn-Pirio said on her website. "It’s about whether deadlines are met, evidence is given to the defendant and victims are spoken to." VIRGINIA DEM DEFENDS SOROS-BACKED PROSECUTOR FROM DOJ PROBE AFTER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGING ALLEGATIONS Fox News Digital reached out to Descano and Dunn-Pirio for further comment. Descano campaign spokesman Nathan Kiker defended the incumbent's record, telling Fox News Digital that "Steve Descano has spent his tenure proving that you can reform the justice system and keep our community safe at the same time." "Today, Fairfax County is recognized as the safest large county in the nation because Steve focused on accountability and the root causes of crime rather than failed policies of the past. We are proud to put that record before the voters," Kiker said. Dunn-Pirio also pointed to "botched sexual assault cases" and prosecutors declining to meet with victims, along with her contention that the justice system too often favors the "well-connected." One case that has drawn the scrutiny of Descano’s office involves Abdul Jalloh, an illegal immigrant from Sierra Leone charged with murdering Stephanie Minter. Minter was stabbed and killed at a Hybla Valley bus stop in February after Jalloh had cycled through the criminal justice system following numerous previous arrests. Descano has pushed back on claims that his office simply allowed Jalloh to walk free, telling Congress his prosecutors obtained convictions against him "wherever possible." SOROS-BACKED DA'S LAX ILLEGAL IMMIGRATION POLICIES LED TO 'PREVENTABLE' BUS STOP STABBING MURDER: COMPLAINT Dunn-Pirio previously served as a prosecutor in Frederick County, Virginia, and as a federal prosecutor in the district covering Lexington, Kentucky. She said she resigned from the DOJ in 2025 after working on COVID-related fraud and similar cases. "I couldn’t stomach propping up a system that gave pardons to the well-connected while prosecuting average Americans for the same conduct," she said, according to a release obtained by FairfaxNow. She also said Descano’s office has spent too much time "failing the people I care about." A carousel on her new campaign website highlights cases that have drawn public scrutiny of Descano, including: REPEAT OFFENDER WITH DOZENS OF PRIOR CHARGES ARRESTED FOR BURGLARIZING CHURCH IN SOROS-BACKED DA'S COUNTY "We need a Commonwealth’s Attorney who can make this office work," Dunn-Pirio said. "Every person in Fairfax should feel safe, and every person in Fairfax should be able to trust the office that’s supposed to protect them." Descano’s campaign did not immediately respond to an additional request for comment on Dunn-Pirio’s criticism. Dunn-Pirio, most recently an associate at the civil litigation firm Harman, Claytor, Corrigan & Wellman, served as an assistant U.S. attorney in Kentucky for two years before resigning in November 2025. At the Justice Department, she specialized in COVID relief fraud and public corruption cases, according to her LinkedIn profile. "Most recently I was a federal prosecutor, and I resigned from the Justice Department because I couldn’t stomach propping up a system that gave pardons to the well-connected while prosecuting average Americans for the same conduct," Dunn-Pirio said. Before becoming a federal prosecutor in 2023, Dunn-Pirio served as an assistant commonwealth’s attorney in Frederick County, an assistant attorney general in the state criminal appeals courts and a law clerk to Judge Randy Bellows in Fairfax County Circuit Court. Dunn-Pirio emphasized that she is a "cradle Democrat," distinguishing her candidacy from a challenge to Descano from the political right. articles.title: Canadian PM Carney says he was prepared for Trump ordering invasion
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he weighed the possibility of a U.S. invasion after Trump began calling Canada the 51st state amid tariffs.
articles.body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he prepared for the "extreme tail risk" that the U.S. would invade Canada amid recent trade tensions. Carney made the statement in an interview with The New York Times published Wednesday, saying he weighed the possibility after President Donald Trump began referring to Canada as the 51st state. "I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk. That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case," Carney told the Times, arguing that "it would be irresponsible not to." CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT Trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada have continued to escalate over the past year, with Trump levying increased tariffs and Canada responding in kind. Carney admitted in a video statement earlier this month that Canada had come to overly rely on its economic relationship with the U.S. in recent decades. FORMER BIDEN AMBASSADOR BLAMES TRUMP FOR CANADA PLAYING 'FOOTSIE' WITH CHINA "The past 40 years has been a period of deeper economic integration with the United States. Truth is, it was easy business, but it meant we relied too much on one economic partner. It’s clear that time is over," Carney said. "This is why our plan, since I came into office, has been development and diversification, not denial, waiting to go back to some good old days and not continued dependence." articles.title: Harmeet Dhillon exposes UC school for discriminating against whites, Asians
articles.summary: Higher education admissions officers desperately want to cherrypick the student population based on skin color, but they are no longer allowed to do so.
articles.body:
Today I’d like to salute Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon, who just caught an elite liberal university red-handed: It seems the University of California San Francisco has been engaged in racial discrimination against white and Asian applicants to the school.

Dhillon writes on X that: “UCSF Med School is 4.6x more likely to admit Hispanic applicants & 12.6x more likely to admit black applicants, than white applicants w/ the SAME academic & socioeconomic backgrounds. Race has no place in admissions & @CivilRights Division will end these illegal practices!”

Now you may remember that race-based admissions were finally ended by the Supreme Court two years ago, in the decision Students for Fair Admissions vs. Harvard . In that case, the plaintiffs presented evidence that Harvard had engaged in blatant racism against Asians; admissions officials chose not to admit Asians who had higher scores than other applicants. In reality, Harvard simply wanted to boost the admittance rate for non-Asians.

This is racial discrimination, and it’s wrong, and should be considered illegal under federal civil rights law. The same laws that make it illegal to, for instance, not hire someone because they are Black should also make it illegal to not admit someone to school because they are Asian. Or because they are white. Or because of any other racial reason.

Finally, we have a Supreme Court that agrees, which is why the decision in 2023 finally recognized that race-based admissions were illegal. But despite that decision, UC San Francisco has continued to ask applicants their race and admit them based on their answer. The proof is the result, according to Dhillon. In her press release announcing the finding, she writes:

“UCSF Medical School’s application process has three stages: the Primary Application, the Secondary Application, and the interview. The Department’s investigation found that race is used to determine which students will advance from one stage to the next, and ultimately be admitted. The Primary and Secondary Applications prompt applicants to identify and discuss their race. And while less than 10% of Secondary Applications advance to the interview stage, black and Hispanic applicants were invited to interview at far higher rates than white and Asian applicants, despite having lower MCAT scores and undergraduate GPAs. From 2023-2025, UCSF Medical School admitted black and Hispanic applicants who academically underperformed the average rejected white and Asian student.”

This is plainly illegal. Higher education admissions officers desperately want to cherrypick the student population based on skin color, but they are no longer allowed to do so, in the same way that they are no longer allowed to discriminate against Jewish applicants, another shameful legacy of the American higher education system. Here was Dhillon recognizing this appalling history the other day.

She’s right. The same thing that applies to Jewish students applies to whites, and Asians, and, by the way, would apply as well to Black students and Hispanic students and Native Americans if, for whatever reason, some racist admissions officers were trying to depress the number of accepted students from any of those groups.

Dhillon says that if the school does not bring its policies into compliance, the civil rights department will file suit. I hope she watches UC San Francisco very, very closely.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Alaska has a voting system like no other state; Republicans worry it could cost them in November
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan faces Mary Peltola in Alaska's ranked choice voting Senate race, complicated by a "Decoy Dan" candidate on the ballot.
articles.body: Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is in the middle of a competitive race as he seeks re-election this year in red-leaning Alaska in a midterm showdown that's one of roughly a dozen that will determine if the GOP keeps control of the Senate. Working against Sullivan as he runs for a third six-year term in the Senate is not only a rough political climate facing Republicans but also Alaska's unique electoral system, which includes four candidates from an open primary advancing to the general election and ranked-choice voting. Alaska is the only state in the nation to have a "top four" primary system in which candidates advance regardless of party affiliation. And it's one of only two states, along with Maine, to use ranked choice voting for statewide and federal races. Defenders of the system say it gives independent voters more choices, weakens party control and encourages candidates to appeal beyond their base. SEEING DOUBLE: THE SECOND DAN SULLIVAN ADVANCES IN ALASKA'S CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN Alaska GOP Chair Carmela Warfield has repeatedly referred to the state's electoral system as a "MESS" in social media posts. "It's hurting the Republican Party," veteran GOP strategist Mary Marslender told Fox News Digital. Sullivan is battling former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. The two candidates combined received over 90% of the primary vote. But Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher and registered Republican whom Marslender and supporters of the senator call "Decoy Dan" is also on the general election ballot. A conservative nonprofit group, Americans for Public Trust, claimed that the other Sullivan, who is not related to the senator, was working with Democrats to confuse voters. The Peltola campaign and Daniel J. Sullivan both denied the allegation. The Alaska Division of Elections disqualified him from the ballot, but the decision was overturned first by an Alaska Superior Court judge and later by the state Supreme Court. SIX FORCES THAT COULD HELP REPUBLICANS DEFY HISTORY IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS There is also a third Republican on the Senate ballot: Gerald Heikes. He advanced to the general election when the fourth-place primary finisher, Democrat David Leslie, withdrew from the race. Marslender claimed that the current system has "become an easy way for the Democrats to game the system." Pointing to Daniel J. Sullivan's inclusion on the general election ballot, she said, "That never would have been allowed in the previous old system. … But because there's an open primary, he was allowed to be on the ballot. "Republican primary voters under the old system wouldn't have voted for him, and he wouldn't have been in there." With ranked-choice voting, voters rank candidates by preference, and if nobody receives a majority of first-choice votes, additional counting rounds occur until someone reaches a majority. Marslender said there's a perception that Republicans would unite around the incumbent senator in the general election. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB But, she said, in Alaska, which is the nation's largest and most remote state, "It's really hard to get a statewide message out" due to "the geographical challenges." Alaskans for Better Elections, which supports the system, has been holding events to help voters better understand how it works. "Alaska’s election system celebrates our independence, giving us the freedom to vote for the person who is best for the job," the group highlights on its website. The Senate race wasn't the only contest impacted by the current system. There were also eleventh-hour withdrawals that rocked the races for governor and the U.S. House, which also cast a shadow on the state's unique voting process. Alaska voters get to weigh in when they cast general election ballots to either keep or scrap the current system. Matt Schultz, a Democrat who suspended his congressional bid before the primary, supports keeping the system. But he told the AP, "We need to make things much more transparent and predictable and understandable by the general public so that we can truly have trust in our democracy again." Republican Lesil McGuire and Democrat Tom Begich, former state lawmakers who were both eliminated in the primary for governor, defended the system. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Let’s be clear: We would have faced challenges and might not have advanced in a traditional closed or semi-closed primary. Our election system was not designed to guarantee anyone a win. It was designed to solve a problem: elections in which a narrow, more partisan slice of voters decided the November ballot, resulting in hyperpartisanship that limited progress," they wrote in an opinion piece in The Anchorage Daily News. "We don’t support our current system because it was good for us as candidates; we support it because it’s good for us as Alaskans."

articles.title: California Supreme Court orders GOP sheriff to return 650,000 seized ballots
articles.summary: A Republican California sheriff must return more than a half-million ballots he seized for an investigation into unfounded voting improprieties in a special election last year, the state Supreme Court ruled Thursday.
articles.body: A Republican California sheriff must return more than a half-million ballots he seized for an investigation into unfounded voting improprieties in a special election last year, the state Supreme Court ruled Thursday. Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco in February seized approximately 650,000 ballots from a November 2025 special election on statewide congressional redistricting favorable to Democrats and pushed by Gov. Gavin Newsom. The measure easily passed statewide, and won in Bianco’s county by roughly 80,000 votes. The court called the ballots’ seizure “unlawful,” saying California law requires voted ballots to remain in the custody and control of election officials, even during a criminal investigation. Bianco must also “refrain from further handling of the ballots except as necessary to comply with our order,” the court said in an unanimous decision. Bianco did not immediately comment on the ruling. Bianco’s ballot investigation came as President Donald Trump has repeatedly disputed the results of the 2020 election, citing unsubstantiated instances of fraud. His administration in January seized ballots and other documents from an election office in Georgia. Some Republicans have mirrored Trump’s rhetoric on voting in their states. Election officials and civil rights groups have been following the Bianco case carefully as they brace for the possibility that Trump or his allies may try to seize ballots in November. Bianco said he confiscated the election materials as part of a criminal investigation after receiving a complaint from a local citizens group that the count was off. Local election officials had previously said the complaint was unfounded. Bianco, was running for governor at the time, but he did not make it through the primary. Democratic Attorney General Rob Bonta immediately launched a legal challenge, arguing the sheriff had no authority over election materials and warning the seizure was designed to sow distrust in elections. He ordered Bianco to return the ballots, but Bianco did not. The University of California, Los Angeles Voting Rights Project also sued the sheriff and the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on behalf of several Riverside County voters. The state Supreme Court last month heard arguments in both cases. Newsom on Saturday signed a bill that would prevent anyone from seizing ballots, as Bianco did. Bianco began recounting the vote shortly after seizing the ballots using sheriff’s officials under the supervision of a special master appointed by a court but suspended it days later, citing mounting legal challenges from the state attorney general and the voting rights group. But he has not returned the ballots. Bradley Hertz, who represented Bianco before the court, argued the sheriff had a legal duty to open a criminal investigation after receiving a complaint and he followed the penal code to carry out that investigation, first issuing search warrants in February. Hertz said Bianco has not returned the ballots to the Riverside County Registrar of Voters because those ballots are “evidence.” At the time of the ballots’ seizure, Bianco was one of two prominent Republicans running for governor in a crowded June primary. He did not advance to the general election and later announced plans to run for reelection as sheriff in 2028. Xavier Becerra, a former state attorney general and Democrat running for governor, is part of the UCLA lawsuit to halt Bianco’s efforts.

articles.title: Senate rejects resolution calling to end the Iran war as most Republicans stick with Trump
articles.summary: The same resolution passed the House in July.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Senate on Thursday rejected a symbolic resolution calling for President Donald Trump to end the U.S. war with Iran, with most Republicans siding with the president despite the war’s unpopularity. Just a handful of Republicans joined Democrats in favor of the resolution: Sens. Rand Paul of Kentucky, Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina. But the majority of the GOP voted against the measure, including Sens. Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska, who are in some of the most competitive races. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., was the only Democrat to vote no. The final vote was 49-50. The measure passed the House in July by a vote of 214-208. Prices on gas, diesel, fertilizer and food have all risen in the U.S. as Iran has turned the Strait of Hormuz into a war zone in retaliation against military strikes that began in February. Nineteen U.S. service members have died. A recent NBC News poll found that just 33% of registered voters believe the Iran war was worth it, while 62% believe it was not worth it. By a margin of 57%-24%, voters are more likely to support a candidate who opposes the Iran war. As a concurrent resolution, the measure expresses the view of Congress. Had it passed the Senate, it would not go to the president for a signature or veto, making it a largely symbolic rebuke of Trump’s ongoing war. It stated: “Congress hereby directs the President to remove the use of United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran or any part of its government or military, including potential ground forces in a combat role or used for occupation, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or specific authorization for use of military force against Iran.” While most Republicans in both chambers continue to side with Trump on the war, some candidates in competitive 2026 elections have defected amid negative public sentiment. In recent days, GOP Senate candidates like Mike Rogers in Michigan and Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa have called for ending the war after siding with Trump on it for months. “It’s more than a message,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said of the war powers resolution. “Congress has the constitutional power to declare war, not the president. So that’s the reason it doesn’t go to the White House, because the White House can’t veto the Constitution.” Kaine has led the charge in the Senate to reassert Congress’ power to declare war, hoping to put pressure on Trump. “If you don’t want to listen to us, how about listen to the American public who’s suffering? Listen to the 18 families who’ve lost loved ones,” Kaine said. “Listen to the hundreds of troops who’ve been injured. Listen to the families, the eight who tried to commit suicide in the extended appointment on the Lincoln.” Trump has defended the war as an effort to weaken Iran and prevent the country from building a nuclear weapon. “Just imagine such a vile regime were ever empowered to carry out large-scale terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield. This was the reality we had to confront. A reality that far too many preferred to ignore,” Trump told world leaders in a speech at the United Nations on Wednesday.

articles.title: 4 GOP senators rebel against Trump on Iran war, vote with Dems to rein in authority
articles.summary: President Donald Trump dismissed midterm fears as Republicans defeated a Democratic war powers resolution despite surging gas and diesel prices.
articles.body: Despite voter fury and rising fuel prices, most Republican senators stayed the course with President Donald Trump and his war on Iran in a vote Thursday. Though vulnerable Republicans on the campaign trail broke with Trump earlier this week, calling for an "immediate end" to the war, lawmakers on the Hill stuck with him and defeated another attempt by Democrats to rein in his war authorities as the conflict nears the eight-month mark. Still, there was a group of rebellious Republicans who had consistently voted with Democrats, including Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, Rand Paul, R-Ky. New blood was added this time with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C. REPUBLICANS BREAK WITH TRUMP TO REBUKE IRAN WAR — BUT IT WON'T CHANGE POLICY Tillis, who is retiring at the end of the year, argued his decision to vote for the latest war powers resolution came after the administration again blew past a 60-day deadline to involve Congress. "We know the resolution's not gonna pass, but it is important to start saying, ‘We deserve an update. You better start treating — Congress can be an assistance with this war effort, if you inform us,’" Tillis said. To Tillis’ point, the resolution that failed in the Senate, which passed in the House with seven Republican defectors, would have headed to the president’s desk, where it likely would have been vetoed. And without a veto-proof majority, the effort wouldn't have teeth legally. However, it will hurt on the airwaves in the ads to come. GOP CRACKS WIDEN OVER IRAN WAR AS VULNERABLE CANDIDATES BREAK WITH TRUMP, DEMAND ITS END Thursday’s vote comes as Republicans are getting an earful about the war, particularly over skyrocketing gas and diesel prices, on the campaign trail. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., acknowledged that fuel prices are a growing issue for Americans. "Well, I think people are, there's voter fatigue with high gas prices and high diesel prices in my part of the world," Thune said. "So, that's a frustration, it's an economic frustration, and that's why, again, I hope the administration is laser-focused on trying to get the [Strait of Hormuz] open, get the shipping lights opened up, and help out with that global energy supply, because that ultimately will get prices down," he continued. Three vulnerable Republicans running for toss-up seats this week, Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan, and Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, all requested that the fighting come to an "immediate end" as the war grows in unpopularity with their voters. TRUMP DEFENDS US INTERVENTIONS ABROAD AHEAD OF 'BIG DECISION' ON IRAN: 'SETTLING YEARS OF UNFINISHED BUSINESS' Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., who has acted as the self-anointed traffic cop for the deluge of Democratic war powers resolutions over the last several months, diagnosed the defections as a by-product of reports that U.S. bombs had fallen on an Iranian school and that diesel costs are "going up and up and up." "They are listening to their constituents. They should [have] listened to them before now, because their constituents were saying, ‘Don't get into this thing,’" Kaine said. "But they're finally listening to them. And nothing makes you listen as much as an election staring you in the face." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But Trump isn’t swayed by the effects that the conflict could have on the midterm elections as the GOP fights to keep power in Congress. "The Republican Party is running, and I'll be helping them, but I am not running," Trump told reporters this week. "I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn't even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."

articles.title: Trump admin removes 760K ObamaCare enrollees amid affordability crisis
articles.summary: Cutting access from health programs for folks whose premiums have already skyrocketed this year is insane, especially a few weeks before the midterm elections.
articles.body:
The latest healthcare decision from the Trump administration is putting the affordability crisis right back in the spotlight.

Vice President Vance announced that the administration is removing about 760,000 people from Affordable Care Act coverage , saying they were either “phantom” enrollees or otherwise ineligible.

“We are stopping ObamaCare enrollment for about 760,000 people who we believe are fraudulently enrolled in the program,” Vance said.

Dr. Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, backed him up, saying: “760,000 people, we call them phantoms, because we believe these people don’t exist or don’t know they have coverage. We believe this because we have been writing them, telexing them, walking to them, FedExing them, whatever we believe we could possibly do to get in touch with them. They won’t answer and they have never filed a claim.”

So, you pay for insurance, stay healthy enough not to immediately need it and somehow that makes you suspicious? Fraud in government healthcare programs is a legitimate issue. But not using your insurance is not the same thing as not needing insurance.

People buy insurance precisely because they may go months, or yes, sometimes years, without filing a claim.

ACA enrollment has already fallen substantially in 2026: 19.2 million people signed up for Marketplace coverage this year, down from 21.8 million in 2025. KFF attributes the decline, in part, to the expiration of ACA tax credits, which dramatically raised costs for many consumers.

So, Americans are already dealing with higher healthcare costs, and the administration thinks the best next step is to simultaneously remove hundreds of thousands of ACA enrollees from access to care?

Cutting access from health programs for folks whose premiums have already skyrocketed this year is insane, especially a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing will make the affordability issue in America worse. Inflation is high, everyday essentials like gas cost more, healthcare costs are higher than a year ago and somehow this is a solution.

And yes, we should want fraud rooted out of Medicare, Medicaid and ACA programs, especially when taxpayer dollars are involved, but there is a huge issue with consistency among the Trump administration surrounding healthcare fraud.

At least 21 people convicted of healthcare fraud received a pardon or commutation from Donald Trump so far. Philip Esformes, convicted in a massive $1.3 billion Medicare and Medicaid fraud case, had his 20-year prison sentence commuted. Judith Negron, convicted of money laundering and healthcare fraud in the hundreds of millions also received a commutation. Justice Department records show both still had restitution obligations after the commutations and now they will never pay that money back.

At the same time, the administration has failed to lay out any realistic healthcare solution. In January, Trump unveiled the “Great Healthcare Plan,” which proposed an idea of lowering health insurance premiums but provided no framework on how, then punted the hard work of coming up with specific legislation to Congress, something that has yet to happen eight months later.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Senate GOP defeats resolution directing Trump to end Iran war as more Republicans sour on conflict
articles.summary: The Senate on Thursday defeated a House-passed resolution directing President Trump to withdraw U.S. troops from the conflict with Iran, despite growing dissatisfaction among GOP senators over President Trump’s handling of the war. Four Republicans joined nearly the entire Senate Democratic caucus for the war powers resolution, which the House passed in July. But the…
articles.body:
The Senate on Thursday defeated a House-passed resolution directing President Trump to withdraw U.S. troops from the conflict with Iran, despite growing dissatisfaction among GOP senators over President Trump’s handling of the war.

Four Republicans joined nearly the entire Senate Democratic caucus for the war powers resolution, which the House passed in July . But the latest measure, a concurrent resolution, failed in a 49-50 vote.

Centrist Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), an ardent supporter of Israel , was the only Democrat to vote against it.

It passed the House in a 214-208 vote two months ago, when four Republican lawmakers voted for it.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Thursday voted for the war powers resolution for the first time, joining GOP Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Rand Paul (Ky.), who have voted for previous resolutions directing Trump to end the war.

Tillis said the conflict has dragged on for too long without congressional authorization and argued it has become a serious political liability for GOP candidates because of its impact on gas, diesel and fertilizer prices.

“We’re reaching a point to where we just need answers. We got to know what success looks like,” Tillis told The Hill.

He added there has been a “consistently downward-trending negative reaction” from the public since the first strikes against Iran in February.

“We don’t know how long it’s going to go,” he continued. “So, we’re afraid it could be a forever war. It’s a war that’s obviously hurting people economically. Why are we doing this? What is the goal?”

Polls show support for the war dropping among Republicans. A CNN poll conducted by SSRS of 1,206 U.S. adults nationwide this month found that support among self-identified Republicans has dropped by more than 10 percentage points since March.

But Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who appeared undecided earlier in the day, cast a key vote against the resolution, sending it to defeat.

He and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) were holed up in the historic Mansfield Room just off the Senate floor right until Cassidy emerged to vote no.

Cassidy was also spotted deep in discussion with Senate Republican Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) before the pivotal vote.

The Louisiana Republican, who lost his primary for reelection in May, rejected the notion that he was being “worked over” by Thune to vote against the measure, telling reporters any speculation that his leaders were pressuring him was “nonsense.”

Democratic Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (Md.) missed the vote.

Cassidy said last week the Trump administration had made “very little” to “no” effort to consult with members of Congress about the war.

He voted with Collins, Murkowski and Paul in June to pass a House-approved resolution directing Trump to end the war.

That led to a heated meeting between the president and Senate Republicans in the Capitol on June 24, when Trump and Cassidy got into a shouting match. The argument got so intense that a Senate colleague had to pull Cassidy back down into his seat.

Cassidy later changed his position and voted against another Iran war powers resolution that Senate Republican leaders hastily brought to the floor after the meeting with Trump.

He explained that he changed his vote because Vice President Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff gave him the information he needed in a special briefing on the war.

Paul also changed his vote to “present” at the time after Trump vented his extreme displeasure earlier in the day over the House-approved resolution passing.

The Congressional Budget Office released an estimate last week that the conflict has cost the Pentagon $38 billion as of Aug. 1.

But the biggest problem posed by the war for many Republicans has been the impact on gas and diesel prices , which have soared since Trump first ordered strikes.

The national average gas price before the war was less than $3 per gallon and has now risen to $4.50 per gallon. The price of diesel stood around $3.52 per gallon in January and this week hit a record high for late September of $6.52.

The House passed another war powers resolution on Sept. 15 in a 220-204 vote after seven House Republicans joined Democrats in voting for the measure.

articles.title: Bipartisan lawmakers announce 20-30 percent US film incentive package
articles.summary: A bipartisan group of lawmakers introduced legislation Thursday that would create a federal tax incentive for film and television productions made in the U.S. in an effort to keep entertainment jobs from moving overseas. The incentive covers 20 percent of eligible domestic labor costs, with additional credits that could raise to as much as 30…
articles.body:
A bipartisan group of lawmakers introduced legislation Thursday that would create a federal tax incentive for film and television productions made in the U.S. in an effort to keep entertainment jobs from moving overseas.

The incentive covers 20 percent of eligible domestic labor costs, with additional credits that could raise to as much as 30 percent. It also stacks on top of existing state film incentives.

“If we want to keep American storytelling in America, we have to level the playing field, and that’s exactly what this bill does,” Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas), one of the bill’s sponsors, said in a statement.

“This isn’t about subsidizing Hollywood — it’s about supporting the American worker, one story and one production at a time,” he added.

President Trump backed the idea earlier this month, calling on Congress to move quickly on a federal incentive. Actor Jon Voight, whom Trump named as one of his “special ambassadors” to Hollywood, has also backed the effort .

The “Deliverance” star pointed to a report from Olsberg SPI released by the Motion Picture Association that found that such a credit could add nearly 150,000 jobs annually across the U.S. while boosting domestic production expenditures by more than $125 billion in the next decade.

Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), another sponsor, said the measure is aimed at keeping jobs and investment in the country.

“We cannot stand by as more and more American film production moves overseas, taking jobs, investment and an important source of American cultural influence with it,” Scott said.

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), who has pushed for a federal incentive for years, said lawmakers now have “the best opportunity in decades to get it done.”

The Olsberg SPI report found the U.S. accounted for an estimated 34 percent of global film production spending and 42 percent of television production spending last year. Researchers projected those shares would continue to decline without a federal incentive.

Global competition for productions has grown in recent years. According to the report, the number of film and television incentive programs worldwide increased from 86 to 121 in 2026, and 65 countries now offer incentives at the national level.

The U.S. currently has no national programs, though 39 states offer their own film and television incentives, which the proposed federal credit would supplement.

articles.title: Almost half of younger voters view capitalism negatively: Poll
articles.summary: Nearly half of younger voters have a negative view toward capitalism, according to a new poll. In the NBC News poll, 47 percent of voter respondents in the age range of 18 to 29 had a negative outlook on capitalism, while 42 percent viewed socialism in a positive light, according to a report from the…
articles.body:
Nearly half of younger voters have a negative view toward capitalism, according to a new poll.

In the NBC News poll, 47 percent of voter respondents in the age range of 18 to 29 had a negative outlook on capitalism, while 42 percent viewed socialism in a positive light, according to a report from the outlet .

Overall, 21 percent of respondents to the poll said they either see socialism in a “very positive” or “somewhat positive” light, while 48 percent said the same of capitalism. Twenty-three percent in the poll said they see socialism in a “neutral” light, while 52 percent said they see it in a “very negative” or “somewhat negative” light.

The poll follows a primary season this election cycle that saw the rise of some democratic socialist and progressive candidates.

Two of the most prominent members of the party at the moment, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D), are democratic socialists. Ocasio-Cortez is also one of the most-discussed names when it comes to the potential Democratic presidential field for 2028.

The poll also comes amid wider concerns about the economy and the cost of living, with oil and gas prices rising over the last year because of the war in Iran. According to AAA, the average price of a regular gallon of gas in the U.S. Thursday afternoon was about $4.48, up from about $3.16 at the same time last year .

The NBC News poll took place Sept. 11-15 among 1,000 registered voters and a had margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

articles.title: California Supreme Court rules sheriff who ran for governor must return seized ballots
articles.summary: The California Supreme Court ruled Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco, a former California gubernatorial candidate, must return approximately 650,000 ballots he seized earlier this year. The court ruled that Bianco’s seizure was “unlawful” as California law dictates that “‘[i]n no event’ shall voted ballots be ‘taken from the custody of the elections official.’” “If election…
articles.body:
The California Supreme Court ruled Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco, a former California gubernatorial candidate, must return approximately 650,000 ballots he seized earlier this year.

The court ruled that Bianco’s seizure was “unlawful” as California law dictates that “‘[i]n no event’ shall voted ballots be ‘taken from the custody of the elections official.'”

“If election misconduct is suspected, the Elections Code provides several mechanisms for law enforcement to review and examine ballots without compromising their integrity,” the court wrote. “But those procedures were not followed and the type of seizure that occurred here directly conflicts with the Elections Code’s carefully considered and controlling provisions.”

The court ordered Bianco to return all of ballots he seized and “refrain from further handling of the ballots except as necessary to comply with this order.”

“Election fraud can and should be investigated,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) said in a statement . “But misuse of criminal investigative tools — without any evidence that a crime was committed — needlessly undermines trust in our elections system and in law enforcement.”

In March, Bianco seized the ballots from a November special election to approve redrawing congressional districts in a way that favored Democrats. He defended his actions at the time as it was part of a criminal investigation into election fraud.

He claimed the results of the election were off by 45,800 votes, but Bonta and Art Tinoco, the registrar of voters for Riverside County Board of Supervisors, argued the difference was only about 100 votes.

Bianco paused the investigation “because of the politically motivated lawsuits and court filings,” according to Los Angeles Times .

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) stated in a press release that the ruling “affirms that in California we will defend democracy — using every branch of government.”

“People deserve to know their ballot is counted and secure, and in California we will do everything we can to protect that constitutional right — this year, and beyond,” he added.

Newsom also signed into law a legislation package aimed at safeguarding the state’s election process against potential interference — targeting actions like Bianco’s seizure.

The new congressional map will be used in the upcoming 2026 midterm elections along with the 2028 and 2030 elections.

The Riverside County Sheriff’s Office did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: Marshall GOP primary challenger backs Democrat in Kansas Senate race
articles.summary: Arch Naramore, who mounted a primary challenge to GOP Sen. Roger Marshall (Kan.) earlier this year, endorsed the senator’s Democratic opponent Thursday. Naramore said in a YouTube video he has “always” been a Republican. But he still threw his support behind Democrat Adam Hamilton, who is seeking to unseat Marshall in the Senate this November.…
articles.body:
Arch Naramore, who mounted a primary challenge to GOP Sen. Roger Marshall (Kan.) earlier this year, endorsed the senator’s Democratic opponent Thursday.

Naramore said in a YouTube video he has “always” been a Republican. But he still threw his support behind Democrat Adam Hamilton, who is seeking to unseat Marshall in the Senate this November.

Marshall comfortably defeated Naramore in the August primary , but the challenger received more than 20 percent of the vote . Naramore noted that point in the video, saying a “lot of Republicans agreed” with him that “somebody” had to take on the first-term senator.

“Roger Marshall went along with tariffs that hurt Kansas farmers. He voted to give billions of dollars in tax breaks to data centers,” he remarked.

The Hill has reached out to a spokesperson for the Marshall campaign for comment.

Hamilton, the senior pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, is attempting to be the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas since former Sen. George McGill in 1932.

The Hill’s polling partner, Decision Desk HQ , gave Hamilton a 23 percent chance of doing so as of Wednesday. The Cook Political Report also rates the race as a “lean” in Marshall’s favor, although the election handicapper shifted the contest to the left Wednesday.

Naramore, who has never held elected office , said Hamilton is “not a politician” and “will fight for all of us: Republicans, Democrats and independents.”

Sharing Naramore’s endorsement video on social platform X , Hamilton wrote, “Kansans of every political party agree: Roger Marshall isn’t getting the job done.”

Naramore is not the only Republican to publicly back Hamilton over Marshall. Former Kansas Gov. Bill Graves (R) endorsed Hamilton last week , saying it is “time” for voters in the state to “do something different.”

“For the last six years, Senator Roger Marshall has turned his back on Kansas,” the former governor remarked in a video Hamilton shared on X.

articles.title: Pro-Trump TV ad funded by government draws fire from both sides
articles.summary: Democrats and some Republicans are criticizing an ad from the Trump administration paid for by the U.S. government that pushes back against communism, socialism and Marxism in the U.S. just weeks before the midterm elections. The 30-second commercial features Trump’s voice, saying, “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” and, “America will…
articles.body:
Democrats and some Republicans are criticizing an ad from the Trump administration paid for by the U.S. government that pushes back against communism, socialism and Marxism in the U.S. just weeks before the midterm elections.

The 30-second commercial features Trump’s voice, saying, “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” and, “America will never be a communist country.” The song “Love Me” by JMSN, whose name is Christian Berishaj, plays in the background.

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) said the ad violated the Hatch Act.

“This may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes,” he wrote on the social platform X. “It is a Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it.

“It is blatantly unethical under numerous federal ethics provisions proscribing the use of government resources for political campaigns,” he continued.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said the ad is “inappropriate” and compared it to something Viktor Orbán, the right-wing Hungarian former prime minister, would do.

“It’s not like they need a GoFundMe page to have the dollars to do that sort of ad and they could do it. But using taxpayer dollars, it feels like Viktor Orbán,” Tillis told reporters.

Trump is not on the ballot in the November elections. The ad does not explicitly urge viewers to vote for any political candidates.

The White House defended the ad, saying the “PSAs are clearly not political.”

“The president is not on the ballot and the ads don’t have a call to action,” a White House official said.

In the ad, photos and videos of the president quickly flash by, touting the “largest tax cuts in history,” along with “reigniting American manufacturing” and “defend law and order and police.”

UFC President and CEO Dana White’s voice also says, “He’s the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met, and nothing was going to stop him from fighting so hard for the country he loves.”

At the end, it says “paid for by the U.S. Government” at the bottom of the screen.

Outlets reported that AdImpact said the advertisement cost $14,000 and ran during conservative shows on Fox News and Newsmax starting Wednesday night.

The Associated Press reported that Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said he hadn’t seen the ad but that he doesn’t “like to see politicians use public money to pay for their own campaign ads.”

A White House spokesperson said the “public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”

“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” the spokesperson said. “We should be proud of our country.”

Berishaj pushed back on the use of his song Thursday, saying he never authorized its use.

“To anybody who has followed my career and knows what I stand for and built my career on, it should go without saying that I would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign,” he wrote on X.

“I’ve built my career independently outside of any major system and have made it a point to not sacrifice my artistic integrity,” he continued. “I don’t have a publicist or anything so being forced in a situation like this and having to comment is ridiculous. I am looking at lawyers and handling this internally.”

articles.body: A mass walkout of delegates before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the United Nations General Assembly prompted a fiery response from the Israeli leader. And for three years, seven fronts Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran, militias in Iraq, militias in Syria, Palestinian terrorists in Judea, Samaria, they all ganged up on us to wipe us off the face of the earth, they failed. "In this battle against the barbarians, we've had no greater partner than President Trump," said Netanyahu. "I thank him. I thank him for his bold leadership. "He understood that if left unchallenged, the fanatic ayatollahs who chant, 'Death to America, death to Israel,' would eventually carry out their mad fantasies. articles.title: Man shot, injured in Butler Trump assassination attempt dies
articles.summary: A man who was shot and injured during the assassination attempt on President Trump at a 2024 campaign rally in Butler, Pa., has died. Jim Copenhaver was one of two event attendees injured during the attack. One rallygoer, Corey Comperatore, was killed after Thomas Matthew Crooks opened fire in an attempt to end the then-presidential…
articles.body:
A man who was shot and injured during the assassination attempt on President Trump at a 2024 campaign rally in Butler, Pa., has died.

Jim Copenhaver was one of two event attendees injured during the attack. One rallygoer, Corey Comperatore, was killed after Thomas Matthew Crooks opened fire in an attempt to end the then-presidential candidate’s life.

Copenhaver was struck by two bullets in his arm and abdomen, leaving him with nerve damage. He died at 76 years old.

The official House Republican Conference’s social media account shared the news of Copenhaver’s death Thursday.

“We are deeply saddened by the passing of Jim Copenhaver, who was gravely wounded in the horrific shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania,” the GOP account posted.

“Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance,” the post continued. “We join his family and loved ones in mourning his loss and praying for them during this difficult time. May he rest in peace.”

Republican lawmakers took to social media to respond to the news of Copenhaver’s death Thursday.

“My prayers are with the family members of Jim Copenhaver, as they grieve his loss,” Arizona Rep. Andy Biggs (R) wrote in a post . “His passing should serve as continued motivation to provide sufficient answers and closure for the investigation into the attempted assassination of President Trump in Butler, where two innocent lives have now been lost.”

Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), the chair of the House Republican Conference, extended her thoughts to Copenhaver’s family.

“Jim was critically wounded in Butler, Pennsylvania, during the attempted assassination of President Trump,” McClain wrote on social media . “He carried those injuries with strength and perseverance. May he rest in peace.”

articles.body:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) directed Michigan State Police to launch a probe into a vehicle pursuit involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Grand Rapids on Sunday, before the other vehicle crashed and killed the driver.

“Given the circumstances of this incident, the governor has directed the Michigan State Police to conduct an independent review of the law enforcement actions surrounding this situation in coordination with the Grand Rapids Police Department’s investigation,” Whitmer spokesperson Kaylie Hanson told The Hill on Thursday.

The Detroit Free Press first reported about Whitmer’s directive to Michigan State Police on Thursday.

Mario David Coronado Juarez, who was alone in the vehicle, was killed in a crash around 7:10 a.m. EDT while driving southwest toward Century Avenue and McKendrick Street before his vehicle struck a tree and caught fire, the outlet reported. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

The Hill has reached out to the Grand Rapids Police Department for comment.

“Preliminary information indicates at some point prior to the crash Sunday morning, Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel attempted to stop the involved vehicle and the driver fled,” police said in a statement to The Washington Post .

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson told The Hill that ICE officers tried to stop a “known criminal illegal alien with multiple alcohol-related driving offenses” allegedly wanted for similar offenses in Guatemala. U.S. Border Patrol deported Coronado Juarez in 2021, but he reentered the country.

“As officers attempted the stop to confirm the identity of the driver, the driver of the vehicle fled at a high rate of speed. In the interest of public safety, ICE officers immediately discontinued the enforcement action,” the DHS spokesperson said. “A short time later, officers saw smoke nearly half a mile from the attempted stop and discovered the vehicle had crashed into a tree and caught fire.”

They added that ICE officers attempted to render aid to Coronado Juarez and extinguish the fire before Grand Rapids police and firefighters arrived.

“Officials also estimated that the suspect’s vehicle was traveling well over 100 miles per hour when the crash occurred,” the spokesperson said.

Along with Whitmer, Grand Rapids Police Chief Joseph Trigg also called for Michigan State Police to conduct an independent investigation, the Post reported.

Coronado Juarez was married and had three young children, organizers with the immigrant rights group Movimiento Cosecha Grand Rapids said in a video posted by MLive , a Michigan-based Advance Local news affiliate.

Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.) sent a letter to acting ICE Director David Venturella demanding answers in connection with the crash.

“No traffic stop should end with a fatality,” Scholten wrote. “Something went wrong, and we need to know what and how. I have sent a letter to Immigration and Customs Enforcement demanding immediate answers about what happened and a transparent investigation into facts we don’t yet know, so that we can prevent something like this from ever happening again.”

ICE has faced months of mounting criticism after a series of incidents, including the death of Minneapolis resident Renee Good during an interaction with the agency in January. Her mother, Donna Ganger, said Tuesday she voted for President Trump “under the impression that these agents” protected U.S. citizens like her daughter.

Earlier this week, ICE officers operating in Evanston, Ill., mistook a man “who resembled the target,” before the man said he was a U.S. citizen during a confrontation with the officers. ICE officers left the area after protesters appeared, fearing “they would be attacked,” according to Evanston police.

articles.title: DHS tried to deport Peruvian man to Africa after appeals court ruling blocking third country removals
articles.summary: A federal appeals court late Wednesday had to clarify for the Trump administration that its ruling last week barred them from deporting migrants to third countries, after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials were poised to deport a Peruvian man to the Central African Republic. A three-judge panel for the 1st Circuit Court of…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court late Wednesday had to clarify for the Trump administration that its ruling last week barred them from deporting migrants to third countries, after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials were poised to deport a Peruvian man to the Central African Republic.

A three-judge panel for the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals last week sided with a lower court judge who had found the Trump administration violated the law in attempting to deport migrants to countries other than the one they are from, determining they have a right to meaningful opportunity to contest and raise concerns.

But after their victory, lawyers for the migrants had to return to court to block one of the deportations at issue in the case.

Trina Realmuto, executive director of the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said ICE “plainly stated that they were treating the decision as if it wasn’t in effect.”

“We filed that in response to the fact that they were clearly moving forward with third country removals, notwithstanding the 1st Circuit’s order and opinion on Friday,” she told The Hill.

The Justice Department has since appealed the case to the Supreme Court.

In Friday’s ruling, the appeals court sided with U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy, a jurist who has earned the ire of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) top lawyer.

Throughout the lower court proceedings, Murphy had determined ICE had “unquestionably” violated his order in seeking to deport migrants to South Sudan, a country for which none in the group had any ties.

In February, Murphy found the Trump administration’s third country deportation policy unlawful, saying it “is not fine, nor is it legal.”

On Friday, the appeals court agreed, finding the policy violated the Administrative Procedure Act.

“The Guidance conflicts with the statutory and regulatory provisions governing fear-of-torture claims insofar as it authorizes third-country removals without effective notice and a meaningful opportunity to assert such claims in connection with such removals. The Guidance is therefore unlawful under the APA [Administrative Procedure Act],” Judge Seth Aframe, a Biden appointee, wrote in the decision for the court.

James Percival, general counsel for DHS, made a social media post after the decision was issued — arguing the ruling was not yet in effect.

“The third country deportation policy continues, as the First Circuit’s ruling is not currently in effect. If you claim fear in your home country, DHS has the right to send you elsewhere,” he wrote.

Percival has blasted Murphy for other rulings, accusing him of having “engaged in mutiny against the Supreme Court” in another case involving temporary protected status for Ethiopia.

An email from a Justice Department attorney offered a more technical explanation: While the appeals court upheld Murphy’s ruling, it did not specifically lift their initial stay barring it from taking effect during trial.

The 1st Circuit Court of Appeals “granted the government’s motion for a ‘stay pending appeal.’ An appeal does not conclude until the mandate issues under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 41 returning the case to district court,” that attorney wrote.

It’s a confusing claim, as the day the ruling was issued the case was remanded back to Murphy’s court.

“They kind of refused to acknowledge that they lost in court, so they came up with this technical point, and then the 1st Circuit took that excuse out from under them,” Realmuto said.

An emergency filing from Realmuto on Wednesday night was swiftly responded to by the court, who at 11:30 p.m. wrote that “consistent with this court’s September 18, 2026, Judgment, the March 16, 2026, stay pending appeal is dissolved.”

DHS did not directly respond to questions about whether it had ignored a court order but defended the practice of third country removals.

“Third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets. Additionally, if an illegal alien chooses to file a claim in court refusing to go to their home country, we are required by law to find a safe and secure nation for them to go to. The First Circuit’s sudden decision to prevent these removals, especially given DHS’s two previous victories in the Supreme Court, is as reckless as it is lawless,” the agency said in a statement.

Attorney General Todd Blanche earlier Thursday said they would appeal the First Circuit’s ruling.

“Without even allowing the government a chance to respond, and in the dark of night, a federal appeals court blocked us from conducting all third-country removals of illegal aliens, an entirely legal and invaluable tool to stem the tide of illegal immigration. We will immediately seek relief from the Supreme Court, which previously granted a stay in this very same case,” the attorney general wrote on social media.

articles.title: Beyer says Trump is prepping construction of his arch
articles.summary: A prominent Democrat said Thursday that President Trump appears to be laying the groundwork for construction of his controversial arch just outside Washington. Rep. Don Beyer (D), who represents the Northern Virginia district where the arch would stand, said he visited the site Thursday morning after constituents informed him that construction vehicles had arrived on…
articles.body:
A prominent Democrat said Thursday that President Trump appears to be laying the groundwork for construction of his controversial arch just outside Washington.

Rep. Don Beyer (D), who represents the Northern Virginia district where the arch would stand, said he visited the site Thursday morning after constituents informed him that construction vehicles had arrived on location.

Beyer said he spoke with construction workers operating “heavy equipment,” who told him they were “conducting archaeological work to evaluate the composition of the soil,” in Beyer’s words.

A federal judge earlier in the month had prohibited construction on the site without giving 14 days notice and barred “any activity” without at least 48 hours notice. The judge made an exception for work related to the search for underground artifacts, but Beyer said his visit on Thursday led him to believe more is being done than simple archeology.

“When I asked [the workers] whether this work was a precursor to construction of the arch, they said that they could not answer,” Beyer said in a statement afterward. “The logical conclusion, however, is that the presence of this heavy equipment and additional surveyors is a clear indication that the Trump Administration is preparing to move forward with construction.”

The remarks came on the same day that the administration took steps to fast-track the approval of the arch by abruptly ending the consultations with local government historians that have traditionally accompanied such projects.

The General Services Administration (GSA) describes those consultations — required under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 — as “an integral component” of the process.

“Under Section 106, each federal agency must consider public views and concerns about historic preservation issues when making final project decisions,” the GSA says .

Instead, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation (ACHP), which is leading the impact review, said it will make its recommendations to the Interior Department without weighing the outside reviews.

“Once the Secretary of the Interior considers and responds to the ACHP’s comments, the Section 106 review for this undertaking will be concluded,” the group said Thursday in a statement .

The announcement came after officials in both Virginia and Washington, D.C., sent letters to the National Park Service declining approval of the arch plan without further examination of its impact on historic sites in the vicinity, including Arlington National Cemetery.

Beyer, who has been leading the charge against the arch, said it would be “deeply troubling” if the administration began construction without a fuller assessment of the effects on the region.

“Trump’s arch is illegal and immoral, and the Administration is also under court order requiring 48 hours’ notice before work proceeds,” he said. “Yet, the Administration appears to be pushing ahead with activity at the site even while it still has not done the basic work necessary to understand the consequences of this project.”

Trump proposed the 250-foot arch on the Virginia side of Memorial Bridge as part of his rolling commemoration of America’s 250th birthday. Stirring the controversy, Trump announced earlier in the week that the arch would not merely be ceremonial but would also house snipers, drones and ammunition.

“There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World,” he posted Sunday on Truth Social.
