articles.title: The 2028 implications of Michigan’s Senate race: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Jonathan Allen explains why Democrats with presidential aspirations will be paying close attention to the outcome of the Michigan Senate election.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen explains why Democrats with presidential aspirations will be paying close attention to the outcome of the Michigan Senate election. Plus, Alexandra Marquez identifies an issue that has united candidates in both parties in tight races. — Adam Wollner The 2028 implications of Michigan’s Senate race Analysis by Jonathan Allen Potential Democratic presidential hopefuls are starting to make sure they find their way to Michigan to campaign for Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Former Vice President Kamala Harris was there this week. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a former South Bend, Indiana, mayor who now lives in Michigan, appeared with El-Sayed in August. And Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., has said he’ll be on the trail next month with El-Sayed, a darling of the left wing of the party. It’s less about him than it is about them. That’s because El-Sayed presents a bit of a two-fer in the endorsement game: 2028 contenders can cozy up to the left and advance the party’s goal of retaking the Senate. Whether El-Sayed wins or loses, those who campaigned with him will surely take credit for both the former and the latter come presidential primary season. The other thing that is as certain as death and taxes is that El-Sayed’s performance against Republican Mike Rogers this fall will be treated within Democratic circles as a sign of whether to sprint left or hit the brakes in 2028. After all, Michigan is a crucial swing state, and, if El-Sayed wins, progressives will argue that they have proven a Bernie Sanders acolyte can capture the presidency. He might not even have to win for that case to be made. On the other hand, more mainstream Democrats would take a defeat — flipping a Democratic seat into Republican hands — as a proof point that voters in battleground states aren’t willing to swing too far left. There’s some recent history here. In 2018, the waiting-in-the-wings class of 2020 Democratic hopefuls read anti-Donald Trump enthusiasm and primary victories by upstart progressives as clarion calls to race to the left. Some of them signed up for Sanders’ “Medicare for All” legislation. In the end, though, Joe Biden — who resisted “Medicare for All” and pleas to defund the police — won both the Democratic nomination and the presidency. Did he prove a progressive couldn’t become president? Of course not. But Democratic voters were concerned, after four years of Trump, that they might blow the 2020 election by nominating a more liberal candidate. It’s not yet clear whether they will feel the same way in 2028. But potential Democratic presidential candidates and their aides will keep a close watch on El-Sayed’s performance — even when they’re not campaigning with him — as they try to gauge how to position themselves best for the primary and the general election. 🔴 On the other side of the aisle: Michigan Republicans break with Trump on Iran, AI and data centers, by Allan Smith and Sahil Kapur How corruption is popping up in Republican and Democratic ads everywhere By Alexandra Marquez Amid a knock-down, drag-out fight for control of Congress, one issue is dominating advertising and transcending partisan divides, instead pitting challengers against incumbents: Everyone is running against members of Congress trading stocks. At least one TV or digital ad mentioning the issue has run in the last month in nearly every competitive race for Congress, according to an analysis of AdImpact data. That includes 18 of the 21 House races rated as “toss-ups” by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter and all but one Senate race rated as a “toss-up” or “leaning” slightly toward one party. Members of both parties are campaigning against congressional stock trading, attacking incumbents and alleging they have used their perch in Congress to get rich amid a broader affordability crisis in the U.S. And unlike some other political issues, it’s just as useful in a battleground district as it is in a deeper red or blue district, as independents and voters from both parties throw up their hands at allegations of government corruption. In some places, members of Congress are airing ads promoting support for a ban on stock trading while an opponent or super PAC runs ads tallying up trades the incumbent made, according to public financial disclosures. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Error leads to backlog of tens of thousands of voter registration applications in Texas
articles.summary: Texas officials sent tens of thousands of delayed voter registration applications to county election officials this week after discovering an error, sparking a scramble to process them weeks out from the midterms.
articles.body: Texas officials sent tens of thousands of delayed voter registration applications to county election officials this week after discovering an error, sparking a scramble to process them weeks out from the midterms. The Texas secretary of state’s told election officials last week that a problem with the Department of Public Safety’s system had been uncovered: certain incomplete voter registration applications that were missing some information were not sent on to election officials, potentially leaving Texans unregistered or with out-of-date voter files. The nonprofit news outlet Votebeat was the first to report the problem. State officials started transmitting the records on Tuesday. It’s unclear exactly how many voters were affected, but large counties have reported tens of thousands of registration applications and updates that election officials must process in less than a month before early voting begins on Oct. 19. And more applications are sure to pour in ahead of the Oct. 5 deadline to register to vote in Texas. The state’s fourth-most populous county, Bexar, received more than 45,000 voter registration forms from DPS, and the fifth-most populous, Travis County, received more than 35,000. “While that number may seem high, the Elections team is already hard at work reviewing every application and will be extending hours to make sure all records are updated well before early voting begins,” Bexar County Elections Administrator Michele Carew said in a statement. Chris McGinn, the executive director of the Texas Association of County Election Officials, said he expected populous, urban areas will be hit hardest, because there are more voter registrations to process and people in cities tend to move more often. “There’s going to be a lot of counties that are paying a lot of overtime,” he said, speaking in a press briefing organized by the nonpartisan Center of Election Innovation and Research. McGinn said some of the records may be duplicative — people may check the box to register to vote when they update their driver’s license, for instance — but still need time and attention from election officials. Texas secretary of state spokesperson Alicia Pierce said a voter who did not appear on the state’s rolls but believes they registered to vote can cast a provisional ballot, and election officials can later search DPS records. Texas is hosting several competitive statewide elections this fall. Democratic state Rep. James Talarico is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. And Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa is challenging GOP Gov. Greg Abbott. In a statement, Talarico called the error “unacceptable” and urged Texans to check their voter registration online. “Less than two weeks before the voter registration deadline, thousands of Texans are now in the dark about their voter registration status — even more aren’t aware of this error at all,” Talarico said. “This is what a broken, corrupt political system looks like: Texans follow the rules, register to vote before the deadline, and still risk losing their God-given right to the ballot box because their government failed to do its job.” McGinn said voters might be better off calling their local registrar’s office. Texas’ online system has reportedly had problems this year, with some registrations inaccurately showing up as inactive.
